messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Policy Analyst
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh had been working late one humid evening in his apartment tower in Seattle when the fire alarm began to pulse and the building lights flickered out. At first he assumed it was a routine drill, but within minutes the hallway outside his door filled with the sharp, bitter smell of smoke, and the announcement over the intercom became choppy with static. By the time he reached the stairwell, he could hear people shouting several floors below and feel the crush of uncertainty around him: no one could say where the smoke was coming from, whether it was contained, or which route was safest. What stayed with him most from that night was not only the smell but the bodily sensation of not feeling right in his own skin—his stomach turning, his head light, his legs unsteady as if he might faint. In the weeks afterward, those moments of feeling physically unwell and those sudden, unpredictable shifts in his surroundings became tightly linked in his mind with the thought that he had failed at the most basic task of keeping himself safe.

Before the fire, Minh had been proud of being careful, steady, and composed. He worked as a policy analyst, a job that depended on weighing contingencies and anticipating what could go wrong, and for most of his adult life that attentiveness had felt like a strength. Afterward, it became something much more frightening. When he felt even slightly ill—an uneasy stomach before breakfast, a brief wave of dizziness in a meeting, the kind of fatigue that used to mean nothing—he would become convinced that he could no longer trust himself to judge danger correctly. If his body could betray him without warning, he reasoned, then so could his mind. He had come to believe that his reactions since the event meant that he was going crazy, especially when the fear rose quickly and made his thoughts race in circles. He started checking the office exits whenever the building made an odd sound and scanning his surroundings for signs of trouble, telling himself that he had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. That vigilance felt protective to him, but it also confirmed, each time he did it, how unsafe the world now seemed.

The smell of smoke was the most immediate way the memory returned. If a neighbor’s barbecue drifted through the apartment courtyard, or if a passing car left a hot exhaust smell near the parking garage, Minh would feel his chest tighten before he had fully identified the source. In those moments he became certain that his body’s alarm was accurate and that he could not rely on himself to stay calm or to make a good decision if another emergency came. He began to mistrust his own reactions in ordinary situations, especially when something felt off but he could not explain why, and that mistrust made him more alert to every faint scent, every flicker of uncertainty. At work, where he spent his days in a quiet government office reviewing reports and drafting recommendations, he started avoiding the conference room closest to the kitchen because burnt toast from the break area could send him back to the stairwell. He would open windows in the middle of winter and excuse himself from meetings if someone mentioned an evacuation plan, a wildfire update, or anything that hinted at unpredictability.

Over time, his life narrowed around these fears. He no longer lingered after work to talk with colleagues, and he had begun asking his wife to handle more of the errands that involved crowded places or unfamiliar routes. He disliked how often he had to apologize for leaving early or seeming distracted, but he was more afraid of what might happen if he ignored the warnings his mind kept sending. The more he watched for signs of danger, the more often he noticed his own racing pulse, queasy stomach, and brief spells of dizziness, and each episode seemed to prove that he was not the man he had been before the fire. The fear of unpredictability did not stay abstract; it followed him into elevators that jerked between floors, into weather alerts on his phone, even into the simple experience of feeling tired after lunch. What had begun as a response to one night in a smoke-filled building had become, in his experience, evidence that he must remain on guard at all times, because a moment of inattention could mean he would freeze, panic, or make some disastrous mistake.

By the time he sought help, Minh was exhausted by the effort of staying careful. He came after a week in which a faint burning smell from a delivery truck in the office parking lot sent him home early, ashamed and shaken, and he realized he was no longer sure how to tell the difference between actual danger and his own body’s warnings. He wanted to believe he could trust himself again, but what frightened him most was the possibility that the next surge of fear would confirm his worst thought—that something in him had broken, and that one more unpredictable moment could send him spiraling further.
